spark.summary: Leader election chooses one coordinator to sequence updates across a cluster while a majority confirms them. It helps replicas maintain one consistent history. The trade-off: failover delays writes and external systems need fencing.
spark.keyTakeaway: A leader coordinates changes. A majority decides. Fencing protects external state when old leaders wake back up.

examples.title: Raft consensus write lifecycle
examples.scenario: A client sends SET user_state = active to Leader Node A in Term 105. Node A appends to its log and replicates entry 8 to followers Node B and Node C.
examples.outcome: Once a majority (Node A + Node B) confirms log storage, entry 8 commits. Replicas apply entry 8 in order, and Node A returns 200 OK to the client.

examples.title: Stale leader partition and fencing
examples.scenario: A network partition isolates Node A. Followers Node B and Node C elect Node B with Term 106. Node A recovers and attempts an external storage write using stale token 105.
examples.outcome: External storage checks the monotonic watermark (106) and rejects Node A's write (token 105 < 106), preventing data corruption.

tradeOffs.pro: Guarantees linearizability and prevents data corruption during network partitions.
tradeOffs.con: Requires consensus round-trips (RTT) and heartbeat leases that limit raw write throughput compared to leaderless systems.

tradeOffs.pro: An odd cluster of 3 or 5 nodes achieves optimal failure tolerance per voting participant.
tradeOffs.con: An even cluster (4 nodes) requires 3 votes for quorum just like a 5-node cluster, providing zero extra fault tolerance while adding network overhead.

tradeOffs.pro: Atomic server-enforced fencing tokens protect external storage deterministically regardless of GC pauses or clock drift.
tradeOffs.con: Downstream storage systems must support conditional version checks or atomic CAS operations.

failureModes.name: Split-brain via asymmetric network partition
failureModes.description: An isolated leader continues servicing writes while a new leader is elected in the majority partition.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce monotonic fencing tokens on all state machine updates and heartbeat leases.

failureModes.name: Election storms via synchronized timers
failureModes.description: Nodes with identical election timeouts transition to Candidate simultaneously, splitting votes indefinitely.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply randomized election timeouts (e.g., 150ms to 300ms) with jitter so one node consistently times out first.

failureModes.name: Stale leader writes to external storage
failureModes.description: A paused former leader wakes up and issues writes to external storage assuming it is still the leader.
failureModes.mitigation: Storage engine enforces atomic token validation: reject any write with a token less than the highest accepted generation watermark.

failureModes.name: Log divergency after partition heal
failureModes.description: Uncommitted entries on an old leader conflict with entries committed by the newly elected leader.
failureModes.mitigation: Raft log matching property: followers overwrite uncommitted conflicting entries with the leader's authoritative log.

commonMistakes: Deploying an even number of consensus nodes (e.g., 4 nodes instead of 3 or 5), providing zero additional fault tolerance while increasing quorum requirement.
Relying on wall-clock time for leases without monotonic epoch fencing, exposing the cluster to clock drift and GC pause anomalies.
Assuming log storage equals execution: replicas apply entries only after learning they are committed.
Allowing stale leaders to write to external systems without fencing tokens.
Omitting pre-vote phase, allowing isolated lagging nodes with inflated terms to disrupt healthy clusters upon reconnecting.

sections.content:
## Why choose a leader?

**Leader election** coordinates state changes across distributed nodes by appointing a single coordinator to sequence writes.

If two nodes both think they are in charge, they can accept conflicting updates. This is called **split-brain**. Raft coordinates decisions using a majority of voting nodes, called a **quorum**. Any two majorities overlap, which—together with Raft’s voting and log rules—helps prevent conflicting decisions.

- **Quorum invariant**: An election requires an absolute majority: $Q \ge \lfloor N / 2 \rfloor + 1$. A cluster of $N = 2F + 1$ nodes tolerates $F$ node failures.
- **Split-brain prevention**: Partitioned minority nodes cannot establish quorum, preventing concurrent conflicting leaders.
- **Monotonic epoch fencing**: Every newly elected leader mints an incrementing epoch token; storage engines reject any lingering write attempts from obsolete leaders.
- **Log replication order**: A follower’s acknowledgement confirms durable log storage, not execution. Replicas apply entries only after learning they are committed, and always in log order.

### Good candidates

- Distributed clusters requiring single-writer coordination (Raft leader, Kafka controller, etcd primary).
- Active-passive database replication systems requiring automated failover.
- Distributed job schedulers or partition orchestrators that demand exactly-once task assignment.

### Think twice

- Stateless web tiers where traffic is evenly distributed across interchangeable worker nodes via L4/L7 load balancers.
- Peer-to-peer gossip topologies where eventual consistency and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) suffice without a single coordinator.

## Follow a write through the cluster.

A client wants to set `user_state = active`. Here is how a three-node Raft cluster turns that request into a committed change.

sections.content:
## How a leader gets elected.

When heartbeats stop, a follower transitions to candidate, increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes from peers.

1. **Heartbeats stop**: A follower waits for its randomized election timeout (e.g., 150ms–300ms).
2. **An election starts**: It increments its term, votes for itself, and asks peers for votes. Peers vote at most once per term and verify that the candidate's log is at least as up to date as their own.
3. **A majority wins**: With $\lfloor N / 2 \rfloor + 1$ affirmative votes, the candidate becomes leader and begins sending periodic heartbeats.
4. **Higher term takes priority**: A leader or candidate that discovers a higher term immediately steps down to follower.

Randomized timeouts reduce the likelihood of split votes. If a split vote occurs, nodes timeout and retry with fresh randomized delays.

## Keep stale leaders out.

A former leader might experience a long GC pause, network partition, or VM migration, then resume believing it still has authority. While Raft prevents it from committing new consensus writes without a quorum, external storage systems need explicit protection.

| Protection Mechanism | How it works | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Monotonic Epoch Fencing | Storage engine validates incrementing token (e.g. token 106 ≥ watermark 106) on every write. | External storage must enforce version checks atomically. |
| Heartbeat Leases | Leader serves local reads while its time-bounded lease is active. | Clock drift or hypervisor pauses can violate lease boundaries. |
| ReadIndex / Quorum Reads | Leader confirms its leadership with a majority before returning read state. | Adds one network round-trip to read operations. |
| Pre-Vote Phase | Candidates verify network reachability before incrementing terms. | Requires an additional pre-vote RPC exchange prior to election. |

## Protect the cluster on a bad day.

### Split-brain via asymmetric network partition

An isolated leader continues receiving writes while a new leader is elected in the majority partition.

Enforce monotonic fencing tokens on all state machine updates and heartbeat leases. Storage engines reject stale tokens.

### Election storms via synchronized timers

Nodes with identical election timeouts transition to candidate simultaneously, splitting votes indefinitely.

Apply randomized election timeouts (e.g., 150ms to 300ms) with jitter so one node consistently times out first.

### Stale leader writes to external storage

A paused former leader wakes up and issues writes to external object storage or databases using obsolete credentials.

External storage must atomically validate and record the highest seen fencing token, rejecting all prior generations.

### Term inflation by isolated reconnecting node

An isolated node increments its term repeatedly while disconnected, then rejoins and forces the healthy leader to step down.

Enable the Raft pre-vote extension: a node only increments its term after confirming a majority would vote for it.

## Quorum arithmetic without surprises

In a cluster of $N$ voting members:

$$\text{Quorum } Q = \left\lfloor \frac{N}{2} \right\rfloor + 1$$

- **3 nodes**: Requires 2 votes to form a quorum; tolerates 1 node failure.
- **5 nodes**: Requires 3 votes to form a quorum; tolerates 2 node failures.
- **4 nodes**: Requires 3 votes to form a quorum; tolerates 1 node failure. An even cluster adds operational overhead without improving fault tolerance.

Any two majorities of size $Q$ in a cluster of $N$ nodes intersect in at least one node:

$$Q_1 + Q_2 > N$$

This overlap invariant guarantees that at most one candidate can win an election in any given term.

## Start small and measure

Deploy odd-sized voting clusters (3 or 5 nodes). Three voters tolerate 1 failure; five tolerate 2.

Tune election timeouts to exceed typical network RTT by a factor of 10. Enable pre-vote to protect against partition disruption, and compact write-ahead logs with snapshots to bound disk consumption.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Leader election chooses one coordinator to sequence updates across a cluster while a majority confirms them. It helps replicas maintain one consistent history. The trade-off: failover delays writes and external systems need fencing.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Node B applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Node C.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Node C experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce monotonic fencing tokens on all state machine updates and heartbeat leases.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: A leader coordinates changes. A majority decides. Fencing protects external state when old leaders wake back up.
Avoid trap: Deploying an even number of consensus nodes (e.g., 4 nodes instead of 3 or 5), providing zero additional fault tolerance while increasing quorum requirement.
Avoid trap: Relying on wall-clock time for leases without monotonic epoch fencing, exposing the cluster to clock drift and GC pause anomalies.
When to reach for it: Distributed clusters requiring single-writer coordination (Raft leader, Kafka controller, etcd primary).
When to reach for it: Active-passive database replication systems requiring automated failover.
